lines.text: אלה 54 אלו
ly before the noun, where it is δεικτικῶς,
Ps. 73, 12. Comp. זֶה. Sometimes it
is thrice repeated, Is. 49, 12.—Like זֶה it
refers also to space, עַד־אֵלֶּה i. q. עַד זֶה
Lev. 26, 18.—Some suppose אֵלֶּה to be
used also for the Sing. as 2 Chron. 3, 3.
Ez. 46, 24. Ezra 1, 9; but these passages
are uncertain. See on this pron. Hup-
feld in Zeitschr. f. d. Morgenl. II. 161.
אֱלֹהַּ, אֱלֹהִים, see אֱלוֹהַּ.
אֲלוּ Chald. see, lo, behold! i. q. אֲרוּ
q. v. Dan. 2, 31. 4, 7. 7, 8. Comp. under
lett. לְ
אִלּוּ if, although, a particle of the later
Hebrew, Ecc. 6, 6. Esth. 7, 4. Syr.
ܐܶܠܽܘ. According to Hupfeld (Zeitschr.
f. d. Morgenl. II. 130) it is i. q. לוּ with
the demonstr. אן prefixed.
אֱלוֹהַּ m. a god, God, with pref. and
suff. לֶאֱלֹהַּ Dan. 11, 38, לֶאֱלֹהוֹ Hab. 1, 11.
Arab. إِلَاهٌ, إِلٰهٌ, c. art. اَللّٰهُ the true
God, Syr. ܐܰܠܳܗܳܐ, Chald. אֱלָהּ. In uni-
son with Aramæan usage, the form of
the singular is employed only in the
poetic style and later Hebrew; while
the pluralis majestaticus v. excellentiæ,
אֱלֹהִים, is the common and very frequent
form.
Sing. 1. a god, i. e. any god, Dan.
So in the proverbial phrase, Hab. 1,
11 זוּ כֹחוֹ לֵאלֹהוֹ this his strength is his
god, spoken of a self-confident person
who contemns God, and trusts to the
strength of his own hand and sword.
Comp. Job 12, 6 אֲשֶׁר הֵבִיא אֱלוֹהַּ בְּיָדוֹ
who carries his god in his hand, i. e. his
sword, weapons. Comp. Virg. Æn. 10.
773 Dextra mihi deus, et telum... Nunc
adsint.
2. More comm. God, the true God κατ᾿
ἐξοχήν, for הָאֱלוֹהַּ, اَللّٰهُ, Deut. 32, 15.
Ps. 50, 22; and often in the book of Job.
Constr. with an adj. sing. Deut. l. c. and
plur. Job 35, 10.
Plur. אֱלֹהִים with pref. contr. בֵּאלֹהִים,
לֵאלֹהִים, כֵּאלֹהִים.
A) In a plural sense: 1. gods, deities,
in general, true or false. אֱלֹהֵי מִצְרַיִם
the gods of the Egyptians Ex. 12, 12.
אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר strange or foreign gods Gen.
35, 2. 4. Deut. 29, 18. אֱלֹהִים חֲדָשִׁים new
gods 32, 17. Sometimes in the language
of common life, both Jehovah and idols
are included under this common appel-
lation; as Ps. 86, 8 among the gods
there is none like unto thee, O Lord!
Ex. 18, 11. 22, 19. But elsewhere the
attribute of deity is expressly denied to
idols, and ascribed to Jehovah alone, as
Is. 44, 6 besides me there is no god. 45,
5. 14. 21. 46, 9. Idols are even called
לֹא־אֱלֹהִים no-gods 2 Chr. 13, 9.
2. Once of kings, i. q. בְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים, Ps.
82, 1; espec. v. 6.
Note. Many interpreters, both an-
cient and modern, assign also to אֱלֹהִים
the signif. angels, see Ps. 8, 6 ibique
Sept. et Chald. 82, 1. 97, 7. 138, 1; and
also judges, Ex. 21, 6. 22, 7. 8. For an
examination and refutation of this opin-
ion, see Thesaur. Ling. Heb. p. 95.
B) In the sense of the Sing. spoken
of one God; see on this pluralis majes-
tatis s. excellentiæ, Lehrg. p. 663, 664.
Heb. Gram. § 106. 2. b. Construed with
verbs (Gen. 1, 1. 3 sq.) and adjectives
singular, as אֱלֹהִים חַי 2 K. 19, 4. 16;
Construed with a verb plural only in
certain formulas, retained possibly from
the usage of polytheism, in which אֱלֹהִים
may perhaps be translated in the plural
and understood of the higher powers
or intelligences. Gen. 20, 13 הִתְעוּ אֹתִי
אֱלֹהִים q. d. the gods caused me to wan-
ment. de Pent. Sam. p. 58.—Hence
1. any god, deity. Deut. 32, 39 there
is no god besides me. Ps. 14. 1. So
where the divine nature is opp. to the
human, Ez. 28, 2. Ps. 8, 6 thou hast made
him but little less than a god; comp.
2. an idol-god, god of the heathen.
Ex. 32, 1 make us a god, i. e. an idol.
1 Sam. 5, 7 Dagon our god. 2 K. 1, 2.
3. 6. 16. So of a goddess, 1 K. 11, 5.
3. the God of any one, is the god
whom one worships, his domestic and
tutelary god, θεὸς ἐπιχώριος. Jon. 1, 5
they cried every one unto his god. Ruth
of Israel is Jehovah, hence very often
called אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל Ex. 5, 1. Ps. 41, 14;

line_status.note: The cross-reference target after "see" is printed pointed and plene: a holem dot stands over the vav and the he carries a patach beneath and a mappiq inside, so Reading A's bare אלוה is wrong; Reading B matches the printed points.
Two vertically stacked dots follow the lamed (sheva), not a single period; no separate full stop is printed.
No vowel is printed under the aleph of אן — neither tsere (A) nor qamets (B); the word is unpointed in the image, while points on neighbouring lines are clearly visible at this scale.
The headword is printed plene: a vav stroke with holem is visible between lamed and he (אֱלוֹהַּ), unlike the defective לֶאֱלֹהַּ on the next line. Reading B drops the vav.

Order of the two Arabic forms: the first printed word has a full-height alif after the lām with a fatḥa above it (plene إِلَاهٌ); the second has only a small dagger-alif over the lām (defective إِلٰهٌ). Reading A reverses them. The article form shows a plain alif with fatḥa, no hamza, as in B.

A damma (small comma-shaped mark) is clearly printed above the final ه of the Arabic word, so اَللّٰهُ with final -u (Reading A) is correct; B omits it. The rest (Hebrew pointing with plene vav and mappiq, Greek, reference) is identical in both and matches the print.
